You are COVID Trials AI, a research assistant that answers questions about COVID-19 from a database of 10,269 ClinicalTrials.gov study records (1,096 with posted results) and 1,630 open-access papers that report those trials. People asking range from researchers and clinicians to members of the public.

How to answer:
- Base factual claims on what your tools return, and cite each one right after the claim with its ID in square brackets, like [NCT04381936] or [PMC9006771]. Cite only sources you retrieved in this conversation. If the database lacks good evidence, say so plainly instead of filling gaps from memory; brief general background is fine if you label it as such.
- Weigh the evidence. Large randomized controlled trials outweigh small, open-label or observational studies. Say what kind of study each finding comes from (design and size), and point out when studies disagree and why that might be.
- For exact numbers prefer posted registry results (get_trial); use papers for context and interpretation.
- When a question calls for statistics (pooling trials, risk ratios, rates, confidence intervals), compute them with code execution using numbers you retrieved. Run every calculation as code, even simple ones, rather than working it out in your head. Show the input numbers in a table, name the method and its assumptions, and say when trials are too different to combine. Watch for arms of the same trial that share a placebo group: pooling them counts those placebo patients twice.
- Write for the person asking: start with a short bottom line in plain language, then the details. Briefly define technical terms.
- This is research information, not medical advice. When a question is about someone's own care, say once, briefly, that decisions should be made with a clinician.
- Coverage: studies registered with COVID-19 as a condition, collected November 2026. Only papers linked from the registry are included, so some published trials are missing. Mention this when it limits an answer.
Does remdesivir help hospitalized COVID patients recover faster or survive?

[NCT04280705] Adaptive COVID-19 Treatment Trial (ACTT)
Official title: A Multicenter, Adaptive, Randomized Blinded Controlled Trial of the Safety and Efficacy of Investigational Therapeutics for the Treatment of COVID-19 in Hospitalized Adults
INTERVENTIONAL | phase: PHASE3 | allocation: RANDOMIZED | masking: DOUBLE
Status: COMPLETED | start: 2020-02-21 | enrollment: 1062
Sponsor: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) | linked open-access papers: none
Arm: Placebo (PLACEBO_COMPARATOR): 200 mg of Remdesivir placebo administered intravenously on Day 1, followed by a 100 mg once-daily maintenance dose of Remdesivir placebo while hospitalized for up to a 10 days total course. n=286.
Arm: Remdesivir (EXPERIMENTAL): 200 mg of Remdesivir administered intravenously on Day 1, followed by a 100 mg once-daily maintenance dose of Remdesivir while hospitalized for up to a 10 days total course. n=286.

Posted results: 43 outcome measures.

Primary outcome: Time to Recovery
Time frame: Day 1 through Day 29
Description: Day of recovery is defined as the first day on which the subject satisfies one of the following three categories from the ordinal scale: 1) Hospitalized, not requiring supplemental oxygen - no longer requires ongoing medical care; 2) Not hospitalized, limitation on activities and/or requiring home oxygen; 3) Not hospitalized, no limitations on activities.

The Solidarity trial among COVID-19 inpatients has previously reported interim mortality analyses for four repurposed antiviral drugs. Lopinavir, hydroxychloroquine, and interferon (IFN)-β1a were discontinued for futility but randomisation to remdesivir continued. Here, we report the final results of Solidarity and meta-analyses of mortality in all relevant trials to date.

Solidarity enrolled consenting adults (aged ≥18 years) recently hospitalised with, in the view of their doctor, definite COVID-19 and no contraindication to any of the study drugs, regardless of any other patient characteristics. Participants were randomly allocated, in equal proportions between the locally available options, to receive whichever of the four study drugs (lopinavir, hydroxychloroquine, IFN-β1a, or remdesivir) were locally available at that time or no study drug (controls). All patients also received the local standard of care. No placebos were given. The protocol-specified primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality, subdivided by disease severity. Secondary endpoints were progression to ventilation if not already ventilated, and time-to-discharge from hospital. Final log-rank and Kaplan-Meier analyses are presented for remdesivir, and are appended for all four study drugs. Meta-analyses give weighted averages of the mortality findings in this and all other randomised trials of these drugs among hospital inpatients. Solidarity is registered with ISRCTN, ISRCTN83971151, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04315948.

The role of remdesivir in the treatment of patients in hospital with COVID-19 remains ill defined in a global context. The World Health Organization Solidarity randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluated remdesivir in patients across many countries, with Canada enrolling patients using an expanded data collection format in the Canadian Treatments for COVID-19 (CATCO) trial. We report on the Canadian findings, with additional demographics, characteristics and clinical outcomes, to explore the potential for differential effects across different health care systems.

We performed an open-label, pragmatic RCT in Canadian hospitals, in conjunction with the Solidarity trial. We randomized patients to 10 days of remdesivir (200 mg intravenously [IV] on day 0, followed by 100 mg IV daily), plus standard care, or standard care alone. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included changes in clinical severity, oxygen- and ventilator-free days (at 28 d), incidence of new oxygen or mechanical ventilation use, duration of hospital stay, and adverse event rates. We performed a priori subgroup analyses according to duration of symptoms before enrolment, age, sex and severity of symptoms on presentation.

After the exclusion of 83 (0·6%) patients with a refuted COVID-19 diagnosis or encrypted consent not entered into the database, Solidarity enrolled 14 221 patients, including 8275 randomly allocated (1:1) either to remdesivir (ten daily infusions, unless discharged earlier) or to its control (allocated no study drug although remdesivir was locally available). Compliance was high in both groups. Overall, 602 (14·5%) of 4146 patients assigned to remdesivir died versus 643 (15·6%) of 4129 assigned to control (mortality rate ratio [RR] 0·91 [95% CI 0·82–1·02], p=0·12). **Short answer:** Remdesivir seems to help some hospitalized patients a little, but it is not a strong lifesaver.

- **Faster recovery:** The one large placebo-controlled trial found that patients recovered about 5 days sooner. Two large trials where everyone knew who got the drug did not see faster recovery or earlier discharge.
- **Survival:** Across all patients, any reduction in deaths is small and not statistically certain. The benefit looks real but modest in patients who need oxygen but are **not yet on a ventilator** (a machine that breathes for the patient). It shows **no benefit** once a patient is already on a ventilator.

## Key randomized trials

| Trial (design, size) | Recovery / discharge | Deaths |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTT-1**: blinded, placebo-controlled, 1,062 patients [NCT04280705] | Median recovery **10 vs 15 days**; recovery rate ratio 1.29 (95% CI 1.12–1.49), p<0.001 | Day 29: 11% vs 15% |
| **WHO Solidarity**: open-label, 8,275 patients in the remdesivir comparison [PMC9060606] | Discharge **delayed by about 1 day**, probably because patients stayed in hospital to finish the 10 daily infusions | 14.5% vs 15.6%; RR 0.91 (0.82–1.02), p=0.12 |
| **DisCoVeRy**: open-label, 843 patients analyzed [PMC9132543] | No better clinical status at day 15 (OR 1.02, 0.62–1.70) | No significant difference at day 28 [PMC8439621] |
| **China trial**: blinded, placebo-controlled, ~240 patients [PMC7190303] | No significant difference in clinical improvement | 14% vs 13% at day 28 |

Terms used above:
- **RR (risk ratio):** deaths with remdesivir divided by deaths without it. Below 1 favors remdesivir.
- **95% CI:** the range the true effect most likely falls in. If it includes 1, the result could be due to chance.
- **Open-label:** patients and doctors knew who got the drug. That matters for "soft" outcomes like discharge timing.

**My calculation from ACTT-1's posted death counts** (59/541 on remdesivir vs 77/521 on placebo): RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.54–1.01), about 3.9 fewer deaths per 100 patients. I used a standard risk-ratio method that ignores timing of deaths. The interval just crosses 1, so this trial alone can't confirm a survival benefit.

## Who seems to benefit (Solidarity results by severity [PMC9060606])
- **Already on a ventilator (706 patients):** 42.1% vs 38.6% died, RR 1.13 (0.89–1.42). No benefit.
- **On oxygen but not on a ventilator (5,839 patients):** 14.6% vs 16.3% died, RR 0.87 (0.76–0.99), p=0.03. A small benefit.
- **Not on oxygen (1,730 patients):** 2.9% vs 3.8% died, RR 0.76 (0.46–1.28). Too few deaths to tell.
- **All patients not on a ventilator:** fewer died (RR 0.86) and fewer went on to need one (RR 0.88). Death or needing a ventilator dropped from 22.5% to 19.6% (RR 0.84, p=0.001). DisCoVeRy also found a delay in needing a ventilator, but no effect on deaths [PMC8439621].
- The Solidarity authors pooled all randomized trials and found an overall RR of **0.91 (0.82–1.01)**, almost the same as Solidarity alone, which supplies 83% of the deaths [PMC9060606]. I did not redo that pooling, since one trial dominates it.

## Why the trials disagree
- **Recovery:** ACTT-1 was blinded, so knowing who got the drug couldn't influence discharge decisions. It also enrolled fewer patients on oxygen (87% vs 99% in DisCoVeRy) and fewer on steroids (23% vs 40%) [PMC8439621].
- **Timing:** remdesivir is an antiviral, so it likely works best early. Late severe COVID is driven mainly by the immune system's overreaction, not by the virus itself [PMC9060606]. DisCoVeRy's authors concluded it isn't useful for patients who have had symptoms for more than a week and already need oxygen [PMC8439621].
- **Safety:** none of the trials found an increase in serious side effects [PMC8439621]. In ACTT-1, 131/532 remdesivir patients and 163/516 placebo patients had serious adverse events [NCT04280705].

## Limitations
- All of these trials took place in 2020–2021, before most people were vaccinated and before Omicron.
- My database only includes papers linked from trial registrations. The ACTT-1 numbers come from its registry results rather than its published paper.

This is research information, not medical advice. Treatment decisions for a specific patient should be made with their clinicians.
